resources.string: Tips
Useful tips
30-Day Tips for Learning the Spring Boot Framework
← Back
Day #1
Understand ApplicationContext from the Inside
Understand that Spring is a container that manages objects (beans).

Create an empty Maven project and add the spring-context dependency. Write a simple Dog class with a bark() method. Create an XML configuration file (applicationContext.xml) describing a bean: bean id="myDog" class="com.example.Dog". In the main method, create the context: ClassPathXmlApplicationContext context = new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("applicationContext.xml"). Explicitly get the bean: Dog dog = context.getBean("myDog", Dog.class). Call the method. Then do the same with Java configuration: create a class annotated with @Configuration, inside it a method with @Bean returning new Dog(). Make sure you did not create objects manually using new (except for the configuration method itself) but requested them from the container.
Day #2
Eliminate the use of the new operator for services
Delegate object creation to Spring

In a real project, never write UserService userService = new UserService(new UserRepository()). Instead, create a UserService class with the @Service annotation and a UserRepository class with the @Repository annotation. In the UserService class, declare a private final UserRepository userRepo field and create a constructor (use @RequiredArgsConstructor if using Lombok). Spring will find the required UserRepository bean and inject it via constructor at startup. This is called "dependency injection" and ensures loose coupling.
Day #3
Master Three Configuration Approaches Sequentially
XML, Java Config and annotations — you need to know all

Create a bean for database connection (just print the URL) using XML. Specify the url property inside the property tag. Create an AppConfig class with @Configuration and a method annotated with @Bean that configures the same component, but using Java code. Add @Component to the class and enable package scanning via @ComponentScan("com.example") in the configuration. Understand how Spring finds classes without explicit declaration. Ultimately, you will be able to read projects of any generation.
Day #4
Experiment with ComponentScan
Package scanning works not by magic, but by clear rules

Create a package structure: com.example.controllers, com.example.services, com.example.utils. Place one class with @Component in each package. Run the application and verify that all beans are created. Now change the base package scan to, say, com.example.controllers. Run again – beans from other packages will not be created. Add explicit specification of multiple packages in the @ComponentScan annotation. Understand that @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan for the current package and all its subpackages.
Day #5
Inject Dependencies Only via Constructor
Field @Autowired (or field injection) is an anti-pattern

Create a service with three dependencies. Implement three options: 1) field injection (@Autowired private Repo1 repo1;), 2) setter injection, 3) constructor injection. Write a unit test (JUnit) for this service. You will see that for the first option, you will have to use reflection or the Spring test context to provide mocks. For the constructor, you simply call new MyService(mockRepo1, mockRepo2, mockRepo3). The constructor explicitly states: "without these three dependencies, I cannot work". In addition, fields can be made final, which guarantees immutability.
Day #6
Study the Bean Lifecycle in Practice
A bean is born, lives, and dies according to a schedule

Create a LifecycleBean class. Add a regular constructor that prints "Constructor". Add a method annotated with @PostConstruct (prints "PostConstruct"). Add a method annotated with @PreDestroy (prints "PreDestroy"). Run the application as a Spring Boot app (so the context lives and dies). You will see the order: first the constructor (object creation), then PostConstruct (dependencies have already been injected, you can initialize resources), upon shutdown, PreDestroy (release resources). Understanding this lifecycle is critical for working with connections, thread pools, etc.
Day #7
Play with Bean Scopes
Not all beans are singletons

Create a Counter class with an int count field and an increment() method that increments it. Make this bean @Scope("prototype"). In a controller or another service, request this bean twice (applicationContext.getBean(Counter.class)). Increment the counter in the first, print it in the second — the values will be different because a new object is created each time. Now remove @Scope (default is singleton) and repeat – the counter value will be shared. Understand when to use prototype (e.g., for thread-unsafe objects or objects with short-lived state).
Day #8
Dive into Annotations for Extracting Data from HTTP
\u0040PathVariable, @RequestParam are request parsing tools

Create a controller that accepts a GET request to /api/users/{userId}/orders. Use @PathVariable Long userId to get the ID from the URL. Add an optional filtering parameter: @RequestParam(required = false) String status. Then make a POST request to /api/users/{userId}/orders with a JSON body that will be converted to an OrderDto object using @RequestBody. Add retrieval of the User-Agent header via @RequestHeader("User-Agent") String userAgent.
Day #9
Centralized Error Handling with @RestControllerAdvice
Don t scatter exception handling across all controllers

Create a custom exception, e.g., UserNotFoundException extends RuntimeException. In the service, throw it if the user is not found. Create a GlobalExceptionHandler class with @RestControllerAdvice. Inside, write a method: @ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class) @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) public ErrorResponse handleUserNotFound(...). This method will catch the exception from any controller and return a nice JSON error message. Add a handler for MethodArgumentNotValidException to handle validation errors.
Day #10
Input Validation Using Bean Validation
Never trust data coming from outside

Add the spring-boot-starter-validation dependency. Create a DTO (e.g., CreateUserRequest). Annotate the fields: @NotBlank(message = "Name is required") String name, @Email String email, @Min(18) Integer age. In the controller, add the @Valid annotation before the DTO. Add a BindingResult parameter if you want to handle errors manually, or rely on the global handler (see tip 9). Try sending a request with an empty name – get 400 Bad Request with an error description.
Day #11
Master Spring Data JPA with a Single Entity
JPA is not magic, but an abstraction over SQL

Create a User entity with fields id, name, email. Add annotations @Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue. Create a UserRepository interface extends JpaRepository\u003CUser\u003E, Long> — no implementation. Enable SQL logging in application.properties: spring.jpa.show-sql=true, spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true. Write a search method by name: List\u003CUser\u003E findByName(String name). See what SQL Hibernate generated. Then add a more complex method: List User findByNameContainingIgnoreCase(String namePart). Understand how method name parsing into queries works. Add a custom method with @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email LIKE %:domain") and @Param("domain") parameter.
Day #12
Configure Connection to a Real Database
H2 is good for tests, but in practice use PostgreSQL or MySQL

Install Docker (or a local database). Run PostgreSQL: docker run --name postgres-spring -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=password -p 5432:5432 -d postgres. Add the org.postgresql:postgresql dependency. Configure application.properties: spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/postgres, spring.datasource.username=postgres, spring.datasource.password=password. Create a table via schema.sql or rely on spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update. Understand the difference between ddl-auto values: none, validate, update, create, create-drop. In production, use validate or manage migrations via Liquibase/Flyway.
Day #13
Implement Database Migrations via Liquibase or Flyway
Database changes must be stored in a repository, not in developers heads

Add the org.liquibase:liquibase-core dependency. Create the src/main/resources/db/changelog folder. Create a db.changelog-master.xml file. Write the first changeset to create a users table (id, name, email, created_at). Add a second changeset to add a phone_number column. Run the application — Liquibase will apply the migrations in the correct order. Check the databasechangelog table where the history is stored. Make sure that on subsequent runs, migrations are not repeated. Understand that this allows you to deploy the database on any environment with consistency guarantees.
Day #14
Understand Transactions with a Real Example
\u0040Transactional is not magic, but AOP with clear rules

Create a service with two methods: saveUser() and saveUserWithLog(). In the first, save the user; in the second, call the first and save a log. Add @Transactional to the second method. Inside, after saving the user, throw a RuntimeException. Run — both saves will roll back because the transaction is atomic. Now remove @Transactional from the second method, leaving it only on the first. Throw an exception — the user will be saved because the transaction does not propagate. Study propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW to create a nested transaction.
Day #15
Configure Caching at Service Level
Caching is the easiest way to speed up an application

Add spring-boot-starter-cache. Add @EnableCaching to the main class. In the service, add @Cacheable(value = "users", key = "#id") above the getUserById method. Call the method twice with the same ID — the first time SQL will be executed, the second time the data will come from the cache. Add an updateUser method with @CacheEvict(value = "users", key = "#user.id") — it will clear the cache on update. Explore @CachePut for updating the cache without invoking the method. Try connecting Redis instead of an in-memory cache: add spring-boot-starter-data-redis and configure the connection.
Day #16
Write Your First Test with MockMvc
Testing controllers in isolation from the context

Add spring-boot-starter-test. Create a UserControllerTest class with @WebMvcTest(UserController.class) and @AutoConfigureMockMvc. Inject MockMvc. Write a test: mockMvc.perform(get("/api/users/1")).andExpect(status().isOk()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("John")). Mock the service via @MockBean: when userService.findById(1L) is called, return a test user. Write a test for user creation: mockMvc.perform(post("/api/users").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content("{\"name\":\"John\"}")).andExpect(status().isCreated()). Ensure the tests run without a real DB and server in seconds.
Day #17
Practice with Profiles
Dev, test, prod environments must be isolated

Create three files: application-dev.properties, application-test.properties, application-prod.properties. In each, specify different database URLs and logging levels. In application.properties, write spring.profiles.active=dev — the dev config will run. Create a bean that should exist only in dev: @Profile("dev") @Component public class DevOnlyBean {...}. When another profile is activated, this bean will not be created. Study programmatic profile activation via mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=prod. Understand how profiles help hide development secrets (e.g., the embedded H2 console) in production.
Day #18
Configure Logging with SLF4J + Logback
Logs are all that remains after a crash

In any class, add private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyClass.class); or use Lombok: @Slf4j. In methods, write logs at different levels: log.info("User {} created", userId), log.debug("Processing request: {}", request), log.error("Failed to save", exception). Create a logback-spring.xml file in resources. Configure console output with a pattern showing date, level, class name. Add a separate appender to write errors to error.log. Set logging levels for different packages: logging.level.com.example=DEBUG, logging.level.org.springframework.web=INFO. Ensure that production logs only INFO and above, while dev logs DEBUG.
Day #19
Explore Actuator for Application Monitoring
You need to know if the app is alive and what is happening inside

Add spring-boot-starter-actuator. In application.properties, expose endpoints: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,env. Run the application and go to /actuator/health – you will see {"status":"UP"}. A load balancer can use this to check liveness. Add custom info: write a bean implementing InfoContributor. Check /actuator/metrics – there are many metrics about memory, threads, HTTP requests. Add /actuator/prometheus if you are setting up monitoring. Configure security: access to actuator should be restricted (management.endpoints.web.port=8081).
Day #20
Explore Asynchrony with @Async
Do not block the main thread on long operations

Add @EnableAsync to the main class. Create a NotificationService with a sendEmail method annotated with @Async. Add Thread.sleep(5000) and a console output inside the method. In the controller, call this method and immediately return "Sending...". You will see that the controller responds instantly, while the email "sends" after 5 seconds. Configure a thread pool: create an AsyncConfig class implementing AsyncConfigurer, override getAsyncExecutor() with ThreadPoolTaskExecutor, setting corePoolSize=5, maxPoolSize=10, queueCapacity=100. Make sure @Async methods are called from another bean (self-invocation does not work due to proxying).
Day #21
Create Your Own Spring Boot Starter
Understand how auto-configurations work internally

Create a separate Maven module my-spring-boot-starter. Add the spring-boot-autoconfigure dependency. Create a MyAutoConfiguration class with @Configuration and @ConditionalOnClass. Inside, create a bean that will be auto-configured. Create a META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports file where you specify the full name of your configuration. Package the starter. In another project, add it as a dependency and verify that the bean was created without additional configuration. Study condition annotations: @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnWebApplication. Understand how Spring Boot enables different configurations based on the presence of classes and properties.
Day #22
Master WebClient for External API Calls
RestTemplate is deprecated, WebClient is reactive and modern

Add spring-boot-starter-webflux. Create a WebClient.Builder bean in configuration. In the service, inject WebClient.Builder and create a WebClient for a specific API: webClientBuilder.baseUrl("https://api.github.com").build(). Make a GET request: webClient.get().uri("/users/{username}", username).retrieve().bodyToMono(UserDto.class).block() – for synchronous call. Study error handling: .onStatus(HttpStatus::is4xxClientError, response -> ...). Try the asynchronous version without .block(), returning Mono\u003CUserDto\u003E. Configure timeouts and logging via ExchangeFilterFunction.
Day #23
Configure Security with Spring Security on a Simple Example
Security is not an option, but a mandatory requirement

Add spring-boot-starter-security. Run the application — all endpoints will be protected with a password that is printed to the console (password generated randomly). Create a SecurityConfig class (use SecurityFilterChain for newer versions). Configure: authorizeHttpRequests().requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll().anyRequest().authenticated(). Add an in-memory user: User.withUsername("user").password("{noop}pass").roles("USER").build(). Add a login form: formLogin().permitAll(). Study how CSRF protection works for POST requests.
Day #24
Implement JWT Authentication Manually
Understanding JWT prevents security mistakes

Add the jjwt-api, jjwt-impl, jjwt-jackson dependencies. Create a JwtService class with generateToken() and validateToken() methods. Use a secret key stored in an environment variable. Create a JwtAuthenticationFilter that extends OncePerRequestFilter. In doFilterInternal, extract the token from the Authorization header, validate it, and set the authentication in the SecurityContext. In SecurityConfig, add this filter before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter. Configure the /auth/login endpoint that accepts username/password and returns a JWT. Test: first get a token, then use it in the header to access protected endpoints.
Day #25
Master the Event Model (Application Events)
Events help decouple components

Create a custom event UserRegisteredEvent extends ApplicationEvent. In the registration service, publish the event via ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new UserRegisteredEvent(this, user)). Create a listener with @EventListener: public void handleUserRegistered(UserRegisteredEvent event) { sendWelcomeEmail(event.getUser()); }. Add a second listener that logs the registration. Run and verify that both listeners are triggered after the user is saved. Study asynchronous events: add @Async to the listener after enabling @EnableAsync. Understand how events work within a transaction: @TransactionalEventListener.
Day #26
Explore File Handling with MultipartFile
File upload is a common task in web applications

Create a controller with a POST method accepting @RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file. Add a check: if file.isEmpty() – error. Save the file: file.transferTo(new File("/uploads/" + file.getOriginalFilename())). Add size limits in application.properties: spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=2MB, spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=2MB. Implement multiple file upload: @RequestParam("files") List\u003CMultipartFile\u003E files. Add MIME type validation: check ContentType so that .exe files are not uploaded as images. Create a download endpoint: return ResponseEntity with InputStreamResource and Content-Disposition header.
Day #27
Configure Second-Level Cache in Hibernate
Entity caching can speed up your application dramatically

Add the hibernate-jcache dependency and a cache library (e.g., ehcache). In application.properties: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache=true, spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.region.factory_class=jcache. Create an ehcache.xml file with cache settings for entities. Add @Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE) to the entity. Run userRepository.findById(1L) twice in a service – look at the logs: SQL will be executed only once, the second time the entity will be from the cache. Study query caching: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.use_query_cache=true. Understand when cache is efficient and when it leads to memory issues.
Day #28
Master Testing with Testcontainers
Real tests on a real database, not on H2

Add the org.testcontainers:testcontainers and org.testcontainers:postgresql dependencies. In the test class, add @Testcontainers and @Container public static PostgreSQLContainer\u003C?\u003E postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer>("postgres:15"). Configure the test DataSource via @DynamicPropertySource: the DB properties will be taken from the container. Write an integration test with @SpringBootTest that actually saves and finds a user in PostgreSQL. Add a test checking email uniqueness – H2 may behave differently, but Testcontainers guarantees compatibility with production. Make sure containers start and stop automatically after tests.
Day #29
Understand Configuration with Condition Annotations
Conditional beans are the foundation of flexible configurations

Create a bean that should only be created if a specific class exists: @ConditionalOnClass(name = "org.postgresql.Driver"). Create a bean that is created only if the property app.feature.enabled=true exists: @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "app.feature.enabled", havingValue = "true"). Create your own Condition: implements Condition, override matches() based on the existence of a file or system property. Apply @Conditional(MyCustomCondition.class). Understand how Spring Boot uses these annotations to enable auto-configuration only when actually needed.
Day #30
Explore Working with WebSockets via STOMP
Real-time communication opens up new possibilities

Add spring-boot-starter-websocket. Create a WebSocketConfig class with @EnableWebSocketMessageBroker. Configure: registry.enableStompBrokerRelay("/topic") for a simple in-memory broker. Create a controller with @MessageMapping("/chat") that receives messages and sends them to /topic/messages using @SendTo. Create a simple HTML client with JavaScript connecting via SockJS and STOMP. Implement sending and receiving messages in real-time. Add connection handling via @EventListener(WebSocketConnectEvent.class). Study how to scale WebSocket connections via Redis.
